questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A grade and the reason attached to it
questions.learningObjective: Connect a grade to the reason given with it
questions.stem: A student receives 62 per cent on an assignment, and the feedback sheet states the grade and then lists three comments without connecting them to the mark.

options.text: Treat the grade as unsupported, because a mark a student cannot connect to a reason is not yet a fair judgment.
Treat the grade as secure, because the mark is the marker's decision and the comments are only illustration.
options.misconception: treats the comments as decoration rather than as the reason for the mark

options.text: Treat the grade as provisional, because the comments will make it obvious whether the mark was right.
options.misconception: assumes the reader can audit the mark from the comments alone

options.text: Treat the grade as generous, because three comments is more feedback than most students receive.
options.misconception: judges the mark by the quantity of feedback supplied

questions.explanation: A grade is only fair if the student can see why it was given, and a list of comments unconnected to the mark does not supply that. Without the connection the student can neither accept the judgment nor work out what to change.
questions.hint: Ask how the student would know why the mark was set.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that tells the student what to do next
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a comment that directs the next step
questions.stem: A peer comment on Amara's literature review reads 'the sources are good, but you need to engage with the counter-argument more closely'.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the comment identifies a gap and points towards the work needed to close it, because 'engage with the counter-argument more closely' names an action the student can take in the next draft. A comment that only named the gap, such as 'the counter-argument is missing', would leave the student to work out what to do, whereas this one indicates the direction of the revision even though it does not prescribe specific steps.

questions.explanation: A comment that names both the gap and the direction of the fix lets the student act on it in the next draft. Naming the gap alone leaves the work of working out the remedy with the student, which is rarely where it belongs.
questions.hint: Ask what the student would do on the next draft.

questions.topic: A comment that names a fault and stops
questions.learningObjective: Spot a comment that stops at naming a fault

stimulus.body: Priya's draft has four paragraphs on a single source, and Josef's comment reads 'source use is unbalanced in this section'.

questions.stem: What is missing from Josef's comment, and who should supply it?

options.text: Nothing is missing, since the comment names the fault clearly and the student can see the paragraphs for herself.
options.misconception: assumes a named fault is enough for a student to act on

options.text: A direction for the fix, such as which paragraphs need more sources or what balance the section should achieve.
A mark, since a fault of this kind should be reflected in the score the student receives.
options.misconception: assumes peer comment must carry a mark

options.text: The other student's approval, since a fault in one draft should be confirmed by a second reader.
options.misconception: assumes fault-finding requires a second reader to be valid

questions.explanation: The comment locates the fault accurately and stops there, so the student is left to decide what balance would look like. The person who read the section is the one who can say what was wanted, and saying so is what turns the fault into a revision instruction.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader was expecting to see in the section.

options.text: The memo should be treated as part of the assessment, since the marker took the trouble to write it at length.
options.misconception: lets the quality of the feedback override the closing date

options.text: The memo should be applied retrospectively, because the student was entitled to feedback inside the timescale.
options.misconception: makes lateness a ground for reopening a closed assessment

options.text: The memo can inform the next piece of work, but it cannot change the grade for a submission that is closed.
The memo should be filed for the record and not shown to the student, since it arrived too late to be useful.
options.misconception: withholds useful feedback because of a timing rule

questions.explanation: Once the assessment is closed its mark is fixed, so late feedback cannot travel backwards to change it. What late feedback can do is inform the next piece of work, and withholding it from the student throws away the only use it still has.

options.text: Leave it, since the marker clearly means the student should develop the conclusion in the next draft.
options.misconception: assumes the marker's intention will be understood unprompted

options.text: Leave it, since the comment shows the marker is being encouraging rather than harsh.
options.misconception: reads tone as the meaning of the comment

options.text: Replace it with 'improve your conclusion', which is shorter and clearer than the original wording.
options.misconception: removes the specific problem instead of resolving the ambiguity

options.text: Rewrite it so the condition is clear, since a student cannot act on a comment that reads either way.

questions.learningObjective: Specify what a revision memo must carry
questions.stem: For her own draft, a student writes a revision memo listing the changes she made, without saying what the changes were for.

options.text: The purpose of each change, so a reader can tell a deliberate response to feedback from a change made for another reason.
The word count of the original draft and the new one, so the memo shows the essay stayed within the limit.
options.misconception: supplies a compliance fact where a rationale is needed

options.text: The names of the people who gave the feedback, so the reader knows who to thank for it.
options.misconception: confuses credit-giving with explanation

options.text: A copy of the feedback itself, so the reader can see the comments the memo is answering.
options.misconception: reproduces the feedback instead of answering it

questions.explanation: A list of changes shows what moved, and only a stated purpose shows why, which is what a reader needs in order to judge whether the revision answered the feedback. Word counts, names and copied comments all sit outside that purpose.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader cannot tell from a list of edits.

questions.topic: What a piece of a portfolio actually evidences
questions.learningObjective: Establish what a portfolio piece actually evidences
questions.stem: A student includes a polished poster in her portfolio, and a reader asks what the piece of work evidences about her practice.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a finished artefact evidences what it presents, in this case design quality and the ability to deliver a polished outcome, and it does not evidence the process that produced it. A poster cannot show how the student made decisions, tested alternatives or responded to criticism, so a portfolio relying on polished outputs alone leaves a reader unable to judge how the work was done rather than only how it looks when finished.

questions.explanation: A finished piece evidences the quality of the outcome and, at most, the skills visible in it. It cannot evidence the decisions, drafts and responses that produced it, so the portfolio has to include work that shows those.
questions.hint: Ask what the finished piece cannot show.

options.misconception: treats the oral as a formality rather than a separate assessment

options.text: Her ability to talk through the work, answer follow-up questions and account for her choices under questioning.
The facts contained in the submitted work, which she can recite from memory without the paper in front of her.
options.misconception: treats recall as the thing the oral adds

options.text: A second opinion from the examiner about the quality of the submitted argument itself.
options.misconception: misunderstands the oral as a source of feedback on the writing

questions.explanation: The oral puts the candidate's own reasoning under pressure in a way the submitted work never does, and that is what the marker is there to assess. Recall of the paper's own contents is already evidenced by the paper.
questions.hint: Ask what the marker watches that a reader cannot check.

questions.learningObjective: Connect a grade to the reason given with it
questions.stem: A marker awards 55 per cent and the only reason given is 'significant work is needed in the analysis'.

options.text: Accept the grade, because the marker is entitled to make a judgment without a full explanation of it.
options.misconception: accepts an unexplained mark as a complete assessment

options.text: Accept the grade, because 55 per cent is a pass and the student can move on to the next topic.
options.misconception: treats a bare mark as sufficient for a learner to act on

options.text: Ask the marker what would raise the work to the next band, because the grade needs a reason that points to action.
Accept the grade but record a formal complaint, since an unexplained mark is unfair to the student.
options.misconception: escalates a request for information into a complaint

questions.explanation: A reason that names what is needed is a starting point rather than a finished judgment, and asking what would raise the work is a legitimate request for the rest of it. Declining to ask, or escalating instead, leaves the student with the same thin reason and a bigger problem.

The comment is complete, because an unclear paragraph is a self-explanatory problem to address.
options.misconception: assumes a named fault is self-explanatory to act on

options.text: The comment is complete, because the marker has identified the fault and the student can judge its severity.
options.misconception: confuses identification of a fault with a usable piece of feedback

options.text: The comment is incomplete only if the paragraph was unclear about the argument rather than the writing.
options.misconception: narrows the incompleteness to a technical sub-case

questions.explanation: Naming the fault is the first half of a usable comment, and this one stops there. A student told that a paragraph is unclear still has to work out what the paragraph should do, which is the part the marker was best placed to say.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Feedback that arrives after the assessed work is closed
questions.learningObjective: Judge the timing of feedback against a closed assessment
questions.stem: A student's undergraduate dissertation is submitted, marked and released, and then the supervisor asks for a correction to a table of figures.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the correction concerns an error in a released result, and the right response depends on whether the error changes the conclusions. If the table is materially wrong, the university has to decide formally whether the mark can be revisited, and the student should be told both that the error was found and what happens next, rather than being left to discover that a published figure was wrong. Nothing in the procedure lets the supervisor change the mark informally.

questions.explanation: Late feedback cannot alter a closed assessment unless the institution has a formal process for reopening it, so the route is a written request through the stated procedure. Leaving the student uninformed about a discovered error is the part that is not defensible.
questions.hint: Ask what the institution's own procedure allows.

questions.stem: What is the risk in this comment as written?

options.text: There is no risk, since praise always carries an implied instruction for a student to take.
options.misconception: assumes students read implied instruction correctly and confidently

options.text: A student may take it as a criticism of the other two sections, which is the opposite of what the marker meant.
The risk is that the comment is too short, so the student will not know it applies to the write-up at all.
options.misconception: treats brevity rather than meaning as the problem

options.text: The risk is that praising one part makes the rest of the marking look unfair by comparison.
options.misconception: redirects the problem to the panel's fairness rather than the reader's understanding

questions.explanation: The comment contrasts the strong section with the other two without saying whether the contrast is a defect or a standard, and a student may hear the second. That is a real risk in a comment that would otherwise be an effective piece of guidance.

questions.stem: A feedback sheet says 'the case study has no counter-argument anywhere in it', and the student has two weeks before resubmission.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the comment locates a real gap, and it becomes usable once it is tied to a response, which in this case means identifying the strongest objection to the case and addressing it. questions.stem: A student writes a revision memo that lists the feedback she received, then lists the changes she made, without saying which change answers which comment.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a revision memo is useful because it lets a reader check that the feedback was actually answered, and that requires the two lists to be linked rather than simply placed side by side. questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that names a fault and stops
questions.learningObjective: Spot a comment that stops at naming a fault

stimulus.body: Hana's feedback sheet contains one comment on her bibliography: 'the referencing style is inconsistent'.

questions.stem: What does this comment do and not do for the student?

options.text: It does both, because the student can correct the style and the comment has told her exactly what to do.
options.misconception: assumes naming the fault tells the student how to fix it

options.text: It does neither, because the comment is too vague to act on and the fault is minor in any case.
options.misconception: dismisses a real fault because the comment is brief

options.text: It names the fault precisely but stops there, leaving the student to work out what counts as consistent.
It does the second but not the first, because the style is only called inconsistent rather than specified.
options.misconception: reads the vagueness as being about the fault rather than the remedy

questions.explanation: The comment says exactly which feature of the bibliography is wrong and nothing about what would make it right. For a house style with a stated rule that is a small gap, but it is a gap, and the student has to close it herself or ask.
questions.hint: Ask what the student still has to determine.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Feedback that arrives after the assessed work is closed
questions.learningObjective: Judge the timing of feedback against a closed assessment
questions.stem: A course publishes a feedback deadline of six weeks after submission, and a student submits a week before the deadline but the marks are released in week nine.

options.text: The student's feedback was late because the deadline was six weeks and the marks came in week nine.
options.misconception: measures lateness without noticing the submission date

options.text: The student's feedback was on time, because the student submitted a week before the deadline.
options.misconception: ignores the actual feedback release date

options.text: The student's feedback was late, because the six weeks runs from submission and the marks came two weeks after it.
The student has no case, because a feedback deadline is a target rather than a commitment.
options.misconception: dismisses a published deadline as merely aspirational

questions.explanation: The six weeks runs from the date the work was submitted, and submission a week early makes the expected release week five, so week nine is late by two weeks. Measuring from the deadline instead would make the same late feedback look early.
questions.hint: Ask what date the six weeks runs from.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment read as the opposite of what it says
questions.learningObjective: Identify where a comment could be read backwards
questions.stem: A marker writes on Nadia's essay: 'the second chapter is where the argument starts to hold together, and the first one is where it does not'.

options.text: That the second chapter should be moved to the front, since the argument only works once it is in place.
options.misconception: prescribes a structural fix the comment does not ask for

options.text: That the first chapter is weaker, so the student should take the earlier chapter first rather than last in her revision plan.
That the first chapter was written last and the second was written first, since the argument was reversed.
options.misconception: infers a drafting history the comment does not record

options.text: That the two chapters are equally good and the marker is describing sequence rather than quality.
options.misconception: reads a comparative statement as neutral

questions.explanation: The comment compares the two chapters and points at the earlier one as the place where the argument does not yet work, which is a diagnostic the student can act on directly. It does not ask for the chapters to be reordered, which is a different and riskier change.
questions.hint: Ask what the comment tells the student to work on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a revision memo has to carry
questions.learningObjective: Specify what a revision memo must carry
questions.stem: A revision memo lists each comment, states the change made and gives a page reference for it, and a reader asks what is still missing.

options.text: The original grade, so the reader can see how much the revision improved the mark.
options.misconception: expects the memo to carry a mark the student does not control

options.text: The marker's comments in full, so the reader can check them without the feedback sheet.
options.misconception: reproduces the feedback rather than answering it

options.text: The revised word count, since the reader will want to confirm the piece still meets the limit.
options.misconception: supplies a compliance fact where a reasoning is needed

options.text: A reason where the student decided not to act on a comment, since declining feedback is a decision that needs recording.

questions.explanation: A memo that records changes answers the question of what the student did, but a reader also needs to see a comment that was considered and declined, and why. A decline is a decision about the feedback, and an unrecorded one looks like an overlooked one.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader cannot tell from a list of changes made.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a piece of a portfolio actually evidences
questions.learningObjective: Establish what a portfolio piece actually evidences
questions.stem: A portfolio contains a tutor-marked draft with comments in the margin, and the reader asks what this piece evidences.

options.text: That the student can work with feedback and revise, because the marked draft and the later version show both the comment and the response.
That the student has good handwriting and a tidy working process, since the comments are clearly laid out.
options.misconception: reads the presentation of the draft as evidence of the student's process

options.text: That the student writes well, because the marked draft is full of the tutor's own words.
options.misconception: mistakes the tutor's writing for the student's

options.text: That the student has a large body of work, since a marked draft and its revision both count towards the portfolio.
options.misconception: counts pieces rather than what they evidence

questions.explanation: A marked draft and the version that answers it are the pair that evidences revision, because they show a comment and a response together. Neither the tidy layout of the comments nor the fact that the tutor wrote them is evidence of the student's own practice.
questions.hint: Ask what the draft and the later version show between them.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an oral presentation puts in front of a marker
questions.learningObjective: Describe what an oral presentation puts before a marker
questions.stem: A module replaces a written submission with a 20-minute presentation and a question round, and a student asks what the marker now sees that they did not see before.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the marker now sees the candidate think: how she structures an argument in speech, how she responds to an unexpected question, and how she accounts for the choices in her own work when pressed on them. Writing lets a student revise, plan and hide the steps that did not work, whereas speaking in front of two markers does not, which is why the oral is treated as a separate assessment rather than a public reading of the submitted script.

questions.explanation: An oral exposes how the candidate thinks and responds, which writing lets them prepare and conceal. That is why the oral is a distinct assessment and not a presentation of the same material.
questions.hint: Ask what speaking cannot let the student prepare for.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A grade and the reason attached to it
questions.learningObjective: Connect a grade to the reason given with it

stimulus.body: A feedback form shows a band of 3 out of 4 and a comment: 'sound grasp of the material, but the reading list is thin and the argument rests on three sources'.

questions.stem: What does this feedback give the student?

options.text: A mark she can query at any time, since the band is provisional until the reading list is improved.
options.misconception: treats a returned mark as provisional and open-ended

options.text: A judgment she can act on, since the band and the comment together say what is sound and what to strengthen.
Two separate judgments, since the band and the comment were written at different times and may not agree.
options.misconception: presumes inconsistency without any evidence of it

options.text: An assessment of her reading list rather than of her argument, since the comment is about sources.
options.misconception: lets one comment define the whole judgment

questions.explanation: The band and the comment work together: the band says where the work sits and the comment says what is sound and what is thin, which is enough for a student to plan a revision. Reading them as two unconnected verdicts, or letting the comment redefine the whole judgment, discards that.
questions.hint: Ask what the two parts of the form add up to.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that tells the student what to do next
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a comment that directs the next step
questions.stem: On a dissertation draft, a peer comment says 'the counter-argument section is strong, and it is the first thing to strengthen'.

options.text: The comment tells the student to remove the counter-argument section, since it is too strong for the rest of the work.
options.misconception: inverts the meaning of a piece of praise

options.text: The comment tells the student to focus on the rest of the draft, since the counter-argument section needs no work.
options.misconception: reads the comment as an exemption for the rest of the work

options.text: The comment tells the student to build on the counter-argument section in the next draft, naming what worked and where to apply it.
The comment tells the student to rewrite the whole draft, since one strong section suggests the rest is weak.
options.misconception: generalises from one comment to the whole draft

questions.explanation: A comment can name a strength and direct the effort towards it, and this one does both. Reading it as a reason to cut, as a reason to ignore the rest, or as a verdict on the whole draft each replaces the comment with a different one.
questions.hint: Ask where the comment is telling the student to spend effort.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that names a fault and stops
questions.learningObjective: Spot a comment that stops at naming a fault
questions.stem: A comment on Teodor's history essay reads 'the second paragraph contradicts the one before it'.

options.text: Nothing further, since the student can see the contradiction and will know to fix it.
options.misconception: assumes the student can see and repair the fault unaided

options.text: A mark adjustment, since a self-contradiction is serious enough to cost a grade point.
options.misconception: turns a comment into a mark and leaves the fix unaddressed

options.text: The two paragraphs rewritten, since replacing the weaker one is the cleanest response to a contradiction.
options.misconception: prescribes a remedy the marker has not judged

options.text: A response that would let the student choose, such as the point at which the contradiction could be resolved.

questions.explanation: The comment identifies the fault exactly, and a contradiction can be resolved in more than one way, so what the student needs is to know which resolution the marker had in mind. Replacing a paragraph, adjusting the mark, or leaving it to her are all decisions taken away from the reader of the comment.
questions.hint: Ask whether the fault has only one possible fix.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Feedback that arrives after the assessed work is closed
questions.learningObjective: Judge the timing of feedback against a closed assessment
questions.stem: A student asks a tutor for feedback on a piece of work that was submitted and closed ten weeks ago, and the tutor replies that the work is no longer open for comment.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the tutor is describing the boundary of the assessment, and asking for a comment on closed work is asking for a second assessment rather than feedback. The student's legitimate need is still real, and the routes that remain open are the ones the institution provides for a final query, an appeal against process, or a discussion of the work in a later piece. The tutor is right that the mark cannot be revisited informally, and the student is right to want to understand why the work fell short.

questions.explanation: Closed work cannot be re-marked informally, so a request for comment on it is a request for a new assessment rather than feedback. The student's underlying need is legitimate and belongs in the later work or in the formal process, and saying so is more useful than a refusal.
questions.hint: Ask what the institution's own routes are.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment read as the opposite of what it says
questions.learningObjective: Identify where a comment could be read backwards

stimulus.body: A comment on Amara's methodology reads 'the sample was small, which is fine if the interview data is representative and only fine if it is'.

questions.stem: What should the student take from this comment as it stands?

options.text: That the sample size is a problem, since the marker is clearly concerned about it.
options.misconception: reads a conditional as a criticism

options.text: That she cannot act without knowing whether the marker thinks her sample is representative.
That the marker thinks the sample is too small and wants a larger one regardless of representativeness.
options.misconception: fixes a reading the conditional does not support

options.text: That the comment is about the interview data only and says nothing about the sample itself.
options.misconception: narrows the comment to one of the two things it names

questions.explanation: The comment makes the acceptability of the small sample depend on a condition the student has to establish, and it does not say whether the marker believes that condition is met. Reading it either way would commit the student to a position the comment does not take.
questions.hint: Ask what the condition in the comment settles.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a revision memo has to carry
questions.learningObjective: Specify what a revision memo must carry
questions.stem: Writing a revision memo, a student explains each change well but does not say which feedback prompted it.

options.text: The link from each change to the feedback it answers, because that link is what lets a reader check the feedback was handled.
A page count of the original draft, so the reader can see how much of the work was rewritten.
options.misconception: supplies a size measure where a correspondence is needed

options.text: An apology for the weaknesses in the first draft, to show the student has taken them seriously.
options.misconception: supplies a declaration of seriousness where a record is needed

options.text: The list of marks the first draft received, so the reader can compare the two versions.
options.misconception: asks the memo to carry a mark the student cannot supply

questions.explanation: The correspondence between feedback and change is what makes a revision memo checkable, and a well-explained change that cannot be traced to any comment leaves the reader unable to see it as a response. Size, apology and marks are all beside the point.
questions.hint: Ask how a reader would check the feedback was answered.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a piece of a portfolio actually evidences
questions.learningObjective: Establish what a portfolio piece actually evidences
questions.stem: A portfolio includes a photographed mock-up of a product the student designed and a written account of why she chose that design.

options.text: Her technical drawing skills, since a photographed mock-up stands in place of technical drawings.
options.misconception: treats a photograph as a technical record

options.text: Her project management, since getting a mock-up made shows she can manage a project.
options.misconception: infers a process skill from the presence of an artefact

options.text: The design decisions she can articulate, and how she defended them, though the photograph cannot show how the design developed.
The originality of her design, since a mock-up that differs from products on sale must be original.
options.misconception: treats difference from market products as proof of originality

questions.explanation: The written account is where the reasoning is visible, so the two pieces together evidence her decisions and her defence of them, while the photograph carries none of that. Neither technical drawing nor originality is something either piece actually shows.
questions.hint: Ask which piece carries the reasoning.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an oral presentation puts in front of a marker
questions.learningObjective: Describe what an oral presentation puts before a marker
questions.stem: A student has prepared answers to the module's published list of questions, and a marker mentions a question that is not on the list.

options.text: The answers she prepared, which the marker can see are thorough and cover the published list.
options.misconception: counts prepared answers as evidence of understanding

options.text: Her listening, since she will have to follow the marker's framing of the unexpected question.
options.misconception: reduces the oral to a skill the marker is not assessing

options.text: Nothing new, since the published list is the agreed scope of the assessment.
options.misconception: assumes the oral cannot reach beyond the published list

options.text: How she reasons when she cannot recall a prepared answer, since that is a thing the written work cannot show at all.

questions.explanation: The unprepared question is the point at which the oral reaches something the submitted work cannot, because it tests reasoning rather than recall. Prepared answers show coverage of the list, and listening shows attention, and neither of those is what the slot is for.
questions.hint: Ask what the marker is seeing when the question is new.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A grade and the reason attached to it
questions.learningObjective: Connect a grade to the reason given with it
questions.stem: A student asks her tutor how the mark was arrived at, and the tutor says the criteria were applied to each section of the work and the marks combined.

options.text: That the mark is a summary of section-level judgments, so a section-level comment is part of the reason for it.
That the mark is a holistic impression and the section comments were only guidance for the student.
options.misconception: treats section-level comments as outside the mark's basis

options.text: That the mark was calculated rather than judged, so the student should recompute it herself.
options.misconception: treats assessment as arithmetic and removes the marker's judgment

options.text: That the mark is provisional, since the tutor has not yet seen the section comments themselves.
options.misconception: invents an unfinished state in a completed assessment

questions.explanation: If the mark is built from judgments on sections, then a comment on one of those sections is part of the reason for the mark. Treating section comments as mere guidance loses the link that makes a particular comment worth reading closely.
questions.hint: Ask what the mark was built from.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that tells the student what to do next
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a comment that directs the next step
questions.stem: A marker writes on a script: 'this paragraph does not do any work', and a student on a study group asks the group what that means for her next draft.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the comment identifies that the paragraph earns nothing, and the useful part is what the student must do instead, which is to say what work the paragraph should do and to cut or repurpose the one that does none. A comment of this kind is hard to act on without a further question, because 'doing work' in a paragraph can mean advancing the argument, evidencing a claim or handling an objection, and the student cannot know which of these the marker had in mind.

questions.explanation: A comment that says a paragraph does not do work identifies a problem but leaves the student to supply the remedy, and the remedy here is a genuine academic decision. Asking the marker which kind of work was expected turns the comment into a revision instruction.
questions.hint: Ask what the paragraph was meant to do.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that names a fault and stops
questions.learningObjective: Spot a comment that stops at naming a fault
questions.stem: A feedback sheet lists three faults in a literature review and no indication of what to do about any of them.

options.text: The comment is finished, because a list of faults is the most useful kind of feedback a marker can give.
options.misconception: mistakes a fault list for a complete assessment

options.text: The student is left to work out the remedy for each fault, which is a decision the marker is better placed to make.
The comment is unfinished only because it lacks a mark attached to each of the three faults.
options.misconception: assumes feedback is incomplete without a number attached

options.text: The comment is unfinished only because the three faults are not listed in order of seriousness.
options.misconception: reformats the requirement rather than identifying what is missing

questions.explanation: A fault list tells the student what is wrong and nothing about what the work should say instead, which leaves the hardest part of the revision with the person least placed to decide it. Marks and ordering would be additions, not the missing content.
questions.hint: Ask who is better placed to decide the remedy.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Feedback that arrives after the assessed work is closed
questions.learningObjective: Judge the timing of feedback against a closed assessment
questions.stem: A module's policy says feedback is released four weeks after the submission deadline, and the deadline for one assignment moves forward by two weeks at short notice.

options.text: The student is still protected by the original policy, because the policy was published in advance.
options.misconception: assumes a published date survives a changed deadline

options.text: The student has no expectation, because the deadline was moved at short notice and everyone knew that was likely.
options.misconception: removes the expectation because the change was foreseeable

options.text: The student is likely to receive feedback two weeks later than the policy promised, because the release date moves with the deadline.
The student should ask for the feedback to be brought forward, because the delay was caused by the module's own change.
options.misconception: treats a policy consequence as if it were an error to be remedied

questions.explanation: The policy measures four weeks from the deadline, so moving the deadline moves the expected release date with it, and the student waits two weeks longer than the policy promised. That is a consequence of the policy rather than a breach of it, which is why asking for it to be brought forward is the wrong remedy.
questions.hint: Ask what the four weeks is measured from.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment read as the opposite of what it says
questions.learningObjective: Identify where a comment could be read backwards
questions.stem: A comment reads 'you have the material and the plan; what is missing is the argument, and it is missing from the first paragraph and the last one'.

options.text: That the middle of the essay is the strongest part, since the fault is named at the beginning and the end.
That the whole essay lacks an argument, since the fault is described as missing from the piece.
options.misconception: reads a local fault as a general one

options.text: That the argument was placed in the wrong paragraph and can simply be moved to the front.
options.misconception: invents a structural remedy the comment does not offer

options.text: That the comment praises the essay's structure, since only the outer paragraphs are mentioned.
options.misconception: reads a fault at the edges as praise for structure

questions.explanation: The comment names the material and the plan as present and the argument as missing at two named points, which means the middle is where the argument does work. Reading the gap as total, or as a misplaced paragraph to be moved, both replace the comment with a different one.
questions.hint: Ask where the comment says the argument does work.

questions.topic: What a revision memo has to carry
questions.learningObjective: Specify what a revision memo must carry
questions.stem: A student has been asked to write a revision memo to accompany a resubmitted piece, and she asks what it has to be able to do.

options.text: Give the reader a summary of what the piece now argues, so they need not read the work again.
options.misconception: asks the memo to substitute for the work itself

options.text: Show that the student has read the feedback, by quoting the comments it responds to.
options.misconception: makes citation of the feedback the memo's purpose

options.text: Record the effort spent on the revision, so the marker can see how much work was done.
options.misconception: asks the memo to evidence effort rather than substance

options.text: Let a reader check that each comment was addressed, including where it was declined and why.

questions.explanation: The job of a revision memo is to make the feedback trail checkable, and that includes the comments the student chose not to act on. A summary of the work, a quotation of the comments and a record of effort each answer a different question and leave the trail untraced.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs to check in the memo.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a piece of a portfolio actually evidences
questions.learningObjective: Establish what a portfolio piece actually evidences
questions.stem: A student submits a portfolio that contains only polished final pieces, and a reader asks what the portfolio as a whole evidences.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a portfolio of finished work evidences the standard of the outcomes and, where the work is visible in them, some of the skills required to produce them. It does not evidence how the student worked: the drafts she discarded, the feedback she acted on, the alternatives she rejected and the mistakes she corrected are all absent, and those are exactly the things a portfolio is usually there to show. A collection of outcomes cannot substitute for a record of practice.

questions.explanation: Polished outcomes evidence the quality of results and little about the practice behind them. A portfolio meant to evidence practice needs drafts, responses to feedback and decisions, not only finished work.
questions.hint: Ask what the finished pieces leave out.

questions.topic: What an oral presentation puts in front of a marker
questions.learningObjective: Describe what an oral presentation puts before a marker

stimulus.body: A module's handbook states that a viva is 15 minutes and that students may bring one page of notes. A student's notes contain a list of quotations with page references.

questions.stem: What does this arrangement put in front of the marker that the notes themselves do not?

options.text: Nothing, since the notes are what the marker will look at and the rest of the slot is formality.
options.misconception: mistakes the permitted aid for the thing being assessed

options.text: Her ability to work without the notes, since the marker is watching how she reasons rather than reading her list.
Her memory, since a candidate who needs a page of notes has clearly not memorised the material.
options.misconception: turns the permitted aid into a test of recall

options.text: The quality of her handwriting, since the marker will refer to the page she brings.
options.misconception: reads the permitted aid as the object of assessment

questions.explanation: The note is an allowance, and a limit on it tells the marker what is being assessed in the rest of the slot, which is reasoning in the candidate's own words. Treating the allowance as a test of memory or as the object of the assessment misreads what the arrangement is for.
questions.hint: Ask why the notes are limited to one page.

questions.topic: A grade and the reason attached to it
questions.learningObjective: Connect a grade to the reason given with it
questions.stem: A marker gives a student a mark of 58 per cent and the reason 'the argument is yours but the evidence is not, and at this level the evidence is what carries the weight'.

options.text: That the mark is punitive, since the comment is about evidence rather than about the student's thinking.
options.misconception: reads a comment about support as an attack on the student

options.text: That the mark cannot be challenged, since the marker has explained the reasoning in full.
options.misconception: assumes a stated reason is the end of the discussion

options.text: That the mark and the reason together credit her own reasoning and locate the shortfall in the evidential work.
That the mark is provisional, since the marker may have intended the comment as encouragement to try again.
options.misconception: reads a critical reason as disguised encouragement

questions.explanation: The reason credits what is the student's and names what is not, and it explains which of the two carries the weight at this level. That gives the student a locatable target for revision rather than a verdict on her ability.
questions.hint: Ask what the reason credits and what it locates.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that tells the student what to do next
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a comment that directs the next step
questions.stem: A marker's comment reads 'you could have pushed this further, and I would like to see that next time'.

options.text: Nothing further, since the comment has already told the student the work could have been better.
options.misconception: assumes a comparison with an imagined better version is actionable

options.text: A list of the specific points she should have developed, which the marker should have included in the comment.
options.misconception: demands the content of a comment the marker chose to give at a higher level

options.text: A mark adjustment, since under-reaching is the fault the comment is describing.
options.misconception: turns an evaluative comment into a mark without evidence for one

options.text: A direction for the next attempt, since the comment names an under-reached ambition as a goal for the next piece.

questions.explanation: The comment sets a standard rather than naming a fault, and it points forward to the next piece, so what the student takes from it is a direction for the next attempt. A list of points, a mark or a bare verdict of inadequacy would each be a different comment, and none of them is the one that was written.
questions.hint: Ask what the comment is for the next piece of work.

questions.learningObjective: Spot a comment that stops at naming a fault
questions.stem: A marker writes 'this literature review is descriptive', and the student asks what a complete version of the comment would include.

options.text: What a critical literature review would do instead, or a prompt for the marker to explain what the review should do.
A mark for the section, since a descriptive review is a failure of a specific kind and deserves a number.
options.misconception: requires a mark where a direction is missing

options.text: A list of the descriptive passages, so the student can find them for herself.
options.misconception: asks the student to locate the fault the marker has already identified

options.text: The definitions of the words 'descriptive' and 'critical', which the student has evidently not learnt.
options.misconception: assumes a knowledge gap the comment does not point to

questions.explanation: The comment names the fault as a whole and stops, so the complete version would say what a critical review does instead, or ask the marker to say so. Marks, passage lists and definitions each treat the label as the problem rather than the missing direction.
questions.hint: Ask what the review should do rather than what it is doing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Feedback that arrives after the assessed work is closed
questions.learningObjective: Judge the timing of feedback against a closed assessment
questions.stem: A student is given the chance to submit one further piece of work after her grade is released, and the tutor says the new work will be marked on its own terms.

options.text: That the released grade can be revised once the new work has been marked, since the two are linked.
options.misconception: assumes a link the tutor has explicitly denied

options.text: That the new work is a fresh assessment, and the released grade stays as the record of the first piece.
That the new work is a re-run of the same task, and the earlier grade is only a stand-in.
options.misconception: misreads a fresh assessment as a replacement

options.text: That the tutor has offered a concession, and the student should take it without querying the terms.
options.misconception: reads an offer with conditions as unconditional

questions.explanation: Marked on its own terms, the new work is a separate assessment and the released grade stands as the record of the first piece. That is what lets the student try again without the earlier mark being at risk, which is the point of the arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask what the tutor said the new work would be marked on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment read as the opposite of what it says
questions.learningObjective: Identify where a comment could be read backwards
questions.stem: A comment on a literature review reads 'this section is the strongest in the portfolio, which is why the rest of it looks thin by comparison'.

options.text: That the rest of the portfolio is weaker, so the student should concentrate her revision there.
options.misconception: reaches the right area for the wrong reason

options.text: That the strong section should be cut, so that the portfolio reads more evenly.
options.misconception: inverts the praise into a reason for removal

options.text: That the strong section sets a standard the other sections have not reached, which is a diagnostic rather than a criticism of them all.
That the comment is about the relative lengths of the sections rather than about their quality.
options.misconception: reads a comment about quality as one about length

questions.explanation: The comment measures the other sections against the standard of the strong one, which tells the student what the portfolio currently lacks and by comparison with what. Reading it as a blanket criticism of the rest, or as a reason to cut the strong section, both lose that diagnostic use.
questions.hint: Ask what the strong section is being used to do.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a revision memo has to carry
questions.learningObjective: Specify what a revision memo must carry
questions.stem: A student keeps a revision memo that is a running log of every change she makes to her dissertation, in the order she made them.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a running log in the order of the changes records the history of the work but not the reason for it, because without the link back to feedback and to the argument the change serves, a reader can only see that something moved. What a revision memo has to carry is the correspondence: which comment or which concern prompted each change, and where she has not acted on a comment, the reason she gave for declining it, since a decision not to act is itself something the reader needs to see.

questions.explanation: A chronological log shows what changed and when, but a reader cannot check whether feedback was answered without the correspondence. The reason for each change, and the reason for any decline, is what makes the memo usable.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader cannot learn from a chronological list.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a piece of a portfolio actually evidences
questions.learningObjective: Establish what a portfolio piece actually evidences
questions.stem: A student includes a peer review she wrote for another student's draft in her portfolio, and a reader asks what this piece evidences.

options.text: That she can judge another student's argument and give specific, useful criticism of it, which is distinct from writing her own.
That she can write well, since a peer review is itself a piece of writing.
options.misconception: treats any writing as evidence of writing skill in the student's own work

options.text: That she understands the assignment, since she had to read the brief in order to review against it.
options.misconception: treats familiarity with a brief as evidence of competence

options.text: That she has collaborated, since reviewing a peer requires working with them on the task.
options.misconception: reads an assessment exercise as collaboration

questions.explanation: A peer review evidences the ability to read another student's argument closely and to criticise it usefully, which is a distinct skill from writing an argument of her own. It is a legitimate portfolio piece precisely because it evidences something the other pieces cannot.
questions.hint: Ask what reviewing somebody else's argument shows that writing does not.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an oral presentation puts in front of a marker
questions.learningObjective: Describe what an oral presentation puts before a marker
questions.stem: A marker says an oral is harder to fake than a written submission, and asks the group why that is.

options.text: Because the questions can be chosen in the moment, so prepared material cannot be relied on to cover what is asked.
Because candidates speak less well than they write, so the oral sets a lower bar than the written work.
options.misconception: misreads a claim about difficulty as a claim about standard

options.text: Because the marker is present, so a candidate cannot submit work written by somebody else.
options.misconception: attributes the difficulty to the presence of a marker rather than to the questioning

options.text: Because oral work is assessed by people who know the candidate's faces, which makes it harder to misrepresent.
options.misconception: reduces the difficulty to familiarity with the candidate

questions.explanation: Prepared material covers the questions the candidate expects, and an oral can ask about anything in the work, so the candidate has to produce understanding on the spot. A lower speaking standard, an attentive audience and an unfamiliar face have nothing to do with it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a candidate who has only prepared answers.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A grade and the reason attached to it
questions.learningObjective: Connect a grade to the reason given with it
questions.stem: A student has a mark of 64 per cent and a comment about the strength of her analysis, and she asks whether the comment is the reason for the mark.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a comment that addresses the analysis is part of the reason for the mark when the mark is made up of judgments on sections, because analysis is one of the things being judged. It would not be the whole reason, since a mark of 64 also reflects the reading, the structure, the referencing and the presentation, and the student should not conclude that fixing the analysis alone will produce a particular figure. The useful reading is that the comment names the part of the work where a gain is available.

questions.explanation: A section-level comment is part of the basis of a section-level mark but not the whole of it, so the student should treat it as the locatable gain rather than the arithmetic behind the figure. Over-reading it either way misleads her about what to change.
questions.hint: Ask what else the mark was made from.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that tells the student what to do next
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a comment that directs the next step

stimulus.body: A marker's comment on a case study reads 'you describe the situation accurately and you do not analyse it; the difference is what the third criterion asks for'.

questions.stem: What does this comment do for the student?

options.text: It tells her the case study is factually wrong, since accuracy is presented here as a fault.
options.misconception: reads the praised part of the comment as the criticism

options.text: It points to the specific criterion her work has not reached, so the revision has a named target.
It tells her to write more about the situation, since that is the part the marker has described at length.
options.misconception: directs her to the part the comment says is already done well

options.text: It tells her the case study cannot be improved, since the marker has found the description accurate.
options.misconception: reads a diagnosis as a final verdict

questions.explanation: The comment names what the work does, what it does not do and where the standard for the difference sits, in a criterion the student can look up. That gives the revision a named target rather than a general instruction to analyse things better.
questions.hint: Ask where in the criteria the missing work is named.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that names a fault and stops
questions.learningObjective: Spot a comment that stops at naming a fault
questions.stem: A marker's comment on an essay reads 'the conclusion repeats the introduction, and the discussion does the work the conclusion should do'.

options.text: The comment identifies two faults and what one of them should be instead, which is as far as it can be taken.
The comment is complete, because the two faults it names are the two that matter in the essay.
options.misconception: assumes a list of faults is a plan for the revision

options.text: The comment is unfinished, because it does not say which paragraph of the discussion is doing the work.
options.misconception: asks for detail the comment was never designed to give

options.text: The comment is unfinished, because it should have said whether the introduction or the conclusion is at fault.
options.misconception: demands a verdict the comment plainly gives

questions.explanation: The comment names two faults and, unusually, also indicates what one of them should be instead, which makes it more usable than a bare list. Asking it to identify the offending paragraph or to rule between the two sections asks for detail it was never designed to carry.
questions.hint: Ask how much more detail the comment already gives.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an oral presentation puts in front of a marker
questions.learningObjective: Describe what an oral presentation puts before a marker
questions.stem: A student prepares for her oral by writing answers to eight likely questions and practising them aloud, and a marker asks what this preparation does not prepare her for.

options.text: It does not prepare her for questions she has not thought of, because eight answers cannot cover a marker's own agenda.
options.misconception: restricts what an oral adds to novelty of question

options.text: It does not prepare her for nerves, since practising aloud removes the effect of nerves on her performance.
options.misconception: assumes rehearsal eliminates a physical effect

options.text: It does not prepare her for thinking on her feet, because the skill being tested is reasoning live rather than recalling an answer.
It does not prepare her for the other candidates, since the oral is a group event and she has not met them.
options.misconception: raises a matter the oral does not turn on

questions.explanation: Rehearsed answers prepare the candidate for the questions she expects, and the skill an oral tests is reasoning through something she has not met before. That is the part the preparation does not touch, and it is the part the marker is watching.
questions.hint: Ask what the marker does with an answer she did not rehearse.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Feedback that arrives after the assessed work is closed
questions.learningObjective: Judge the timing of feedback against a closed assessment
questions.stem: A student is told her master's dissertation has been examined and the mark is pending, and she asks whether the examiner may still comment on the draft she submitted.

options.text: No, because an examined piece is closed work and the examiner cannot reopen it.
options.misconception: treats an open examination as a closed assessment

options.text: Yes, because the examiner has not yet finished with the work and can comment as part of the process.
options.misconception: assumes an examiner's comment is part of the marking process

options.text: Yes, but only on matters of fact, since correcting facts is not a re-marking of the argument.
options.misconception: invents a permitted category of comment nobody has set

options.text: Only if the process allows it, since otherwise the draft is closed and she must use the formal query route.

questions.explanation: Whether comment is possible depends on the process the university has set, and a student cannot assume either answer. If the draft is closed, the formal query route is the way to get an answer, and assuming a comment is available risks relying on something that does not exist.
questions.hint: Ask what the process itself allows.
